Jean de Oliveira


PhD Candidate in EconomicsGoethe University Frankfurt




I am a PhD candidate at Goethe University Frankfurt. I work on the economics of deforestation, with a special focus on Indigenous territories of the Amazon. My research asks how land rights and the financial system shape what happens to forests, combining administrative records with spatial data. I also study household beliefs and expectations, and how they shape financial decisions.


Contact: jeanoli@stud.uni-frankfurt.de

title: Jean de Oliveira
text:
Working Papers

Branches and Roots: Banking Presence and Deforestation in Amazonian Indigenous Lands
Job Market Paper
With Douglas K.G. de Araujo
Indigenous lands shelter much of the Brazilian Amazon’s intact forest, yet illegal deforestation inside their boundaries has been climbing despite formal legal protection. We exploit a sharp expansion and subsequent contraction of the region’s bank-branch network between 2008 and 2024 to ask whether local banking presence affects deforestation inside nearby Indigenous lands. We find that each additional branch near an Indigenous land lowers cumulative forest loss inside that area by roughly 2.5 km² over five years. Mediation analysis attributes the bulk of this effect to a single channel: bank presence raises local social capital, and exogenous variation in social capital in turn lowers deforestation. By contrast, we find no evidence that either local economic conditions or access to capital for clearing transmits the effect.

Actual and Perceived Financial Knowledge over the Life Cycle
What happens when households believe they know more than they actually do about financial matters? I use causal evidence to show that overconfidence leads households to drain their retirement savings early, fall behind on their mortgages, and lean too heavily on credit cards. A calibrated life-cycle model then traces how the damage compounds across the working years and lands hardest in the retirement years.
